Marvel Studios debuted a unique promo for Avengers: Doomsday during Game 1 of the 2026 World Series on Fox tonight between the Milwaukee Brewers and Tampa Bay Rays. The ad is an Avengers-MLB crossover set on Earth-828 at Ebbets Field (the former home of the Dodgers when they were in Brooklyn; it was torn down on our Earth in 1960 – the promo is seemingly set in the same time period as The Fantastic Four: First Steps, as you can see New York Giants players in the background).

In it, Mr. Fantastic, sporting a Brooklyn Dodgers cap, takes the mound to throw a stretchy-armed first pitch while The Thing hypes up the players as current, modern MLB players Freddie Freeman, Jacob Misiorowski, Bryce Harper, Randy Arozarena, and Junior Caminero look on from the sidelines. articles.title: World Series 2026: Brewers jump ahead of Rays early, Jacob Misiorowski and bullpen secure 1-0 series lead
articles.summary: The Brewers won their first World Series game in 44 years.
articles.body: After waiting 44 years for a return to the World Series, the Milwaukee Brewers had to survive a stressful ninth inning in Game 1.A decent start by Jacob Misiorowski, a sharp bullpen performance and an early rally added up to a series-opening 3-2 win over the Tampa Bay Rays on Friday night, even after closer Trevor Megill allowed a run in the ninth and was in danger of allowing more. Milwaukee leads 1-0, much like it did in its last Fall Classic in 1982, which the club lost in seven games.Game 2 is scheduled for Saturday at 8 p.m. ET, with Rays ace Drew Rasmussen and Brewers rookie Logan Henderson set to take the mound. Both teams are in pursuit of their first World Series title.There it is!Brewers officially take Game 1.@MLBONFOX pic.twitter.com/t3zrBgqv2q— FOX Sports (@FOXSports) October 24, 2026 The Brewers had reason to be confident going into the opener. Even with Misiorowski's so-so performances in his previous two starts, he's still the presumptive NL Cy Young Award winner, while the Rays opted to start Nick Martinez instead of Rasmussen on normal rest.Misiorowski opened the game with the fastest pitch in World Series history, and was solid for the next five innings. His lone blemish came thanks to an absolutely scorched line drive from Rays star Junior Caminero, which left the bat at 112.7 mph and had enough carry to fool Brewers center fielder Garrett Mitchell for a double. The Rays got their lone run three pitches later.And with that 103 MPH Miz fastball, the 2026 World Series is underway.📺: FOX, stream on @foxone: pic.twitter.com/g3SMes6SUq— FOX Sports: MLB (@MLBONFOX) October 24, 2026Misiorowski's final line was 5 innings, 4 hits, 1 run, 1 walk and 3 strikeouts on 73 pitches. The Brewers didn't push him into the sixth, instead opting to activate a bullpen that has been nails all postseason. That continued Friday, with Abner Uribe, Aaron Ashby and Megill combining for five strikeouts in four innings.There was concern when Megill loaded the bases in the ninth inning, and even more when a would-be game-ending double play got overturned after shortstop Cooper Pratt's foot left second base. Was Cooper Pratt's foot off the bag on this potential game-ending double play? pic.twitter.com/8JpspjM3HY— FOX Sports: MLB (@MLBONFOX) October 24, 2026 That put the tying run on third base with two outs, but Megill struck out Jonny DeLuca to end the game.On the offensive side, Milwaukee struck early.Martinez is a throwback sort of pitcher compared to the high velocity-dominated era that Misiorowski epitomizes. Martinez usually sits in the low 90s. On a rate basis, he got fewer whiffs than any qualified pitcher in MLB during the regular season, he threw more pitches in the strike zone than any qualified pitcher and he walked the fewest batters of any qualified pitcher.The veteran right-hander pitches to contact, and was facing a Brewers lineup that gets more walks and swings at fewer pitches than any team in baseball. It was a fascinating matchup, and it was the Brewers who wound up drifting from their usual identity.It was to their benefit. The top of the Brewers' lineup came out swinging, with Jackson Chourio and William Contreras both recording hits on their first pitch. Brewers captain Christian Yelich had the big knock between them with an RBI triple and later scored on the Contreras single.THE BREWERS STRIKE FIRST 😤Christian Yelich immediately puts the Brewers on the board with an RBI triple! pic.twitter.com/8xOy2p4Gkk— MLB (@MLB) October 24, 2026The Brewers added an insurance run in the seventh inning on another first-pitch single from Chourio, which wound up being quite important.If there's a consolation for the Rays, this was a game the Brewers seemingly needed more than them. Tampa Bay certainly didn't treat this game as a must-win, opting to use the likes of Steven Matz, Kevin Kelly and Cole Sulser — its three least-used pitchers of the postseason — rather than any of its premium bullpen arms once Martinez was out with a one-run deficit.The Rays might have very well punted on this game, or at least decided this was a matchup not worth over-extending themselves. Game 2 looms as a far more favorable environment, but every alarm bell will be ringing if this series leaves Milwaukee with the Brewers up 2-0.

articles.title: Brewers Survive Rays Rally to Win, Box Score Stats, Highlights from 2026 MLB World Series Game 1
articles.summary: The Milwaukee Brewers took down the Tampa Bay Rays in Game 1 of the 2026 World Series, winning by the final score of 3-2 on Friday night.
articles.body:
The Milwaukee Brewers took down the Tampa Bay Rays in Game 1 of the 2026 World Series, winning by the final score of 3-2 on Friday night.

The Rays successfully won a challenge to avoid a game-ending double play in the ninth inning, but still couldn't complete a late rally to secure a comeback victory.

The Brewers didn't waste time getting on the board, taking a 1-0 lead in the bottom of the first inning with Christian Yelich's RBI triple.

Milwaukee wasn't finished, as William Contreras eventually drove in Yelich with a single.

Both teams were scoreless over the next pair of innings, although Tampa Bay eventually cut the deficit to 2-1 after Jonathan Aranda scored on a groundout by Liam Hicks.

Still, Milwaukee was able to prevent the Rays from tying the contest due to a series of stellar defensive plays.

Jackson Chourio provided the Brewers with some insurance in the bottom of the seventh, as he brought home Cooper Pratt with a two-out single.

With Milwaukee holding a 3-1 lead in the top of the ninth inning, Tampa Bay loaded the bases with just one out.

The Rays scored a run off a groundout by Hicks following the successful challenge, but a strikeout by Jonny DeLuca sealed the final result.

Brewers ace Jacob Misiorowski allowed just one run in five innings of work, as Tampa Bay went 0-for-6 with runners in scoring position.

articles.title: World Series 2026: Dozens of people exit field after Brewers' game-ending double play is overturned on review
articles.summary: Game 1 of the World Series ended awkwardly.
articles.body:
Game 1 of the 2026 World Series featured two different endings, but still resulted in a 3-2 Milwaukee Brewers win .

The Brewers appeared to take a 1-0 series lead after Tampa Bays Rays catcher Liam Hicks ground into a double play with the bases loaded and one out, ending a stressful inning for closer Trevor Megill as he tried to protect a two-run lead.

Players and fans began celebrating, as the usual postgame mechanics of a World Series game began playing out. However, everything had to pause when the Rays challenged the play.

Review quickly showed why. Rookie Brewers shortstop Cooper Pratt had taken his foot off second base quite early as he prepared to throw to first base. Too early, it turned out, as the umpires announced the call had been overturned.

Instead of game over, the Rays had runners on second and third with two outs and Jonny DeLuca up to bat. That resulted in some awkward scenes, as dozens of people — and a few golf carts — had to leave the field for the game could get started again.

Fortunately for the sanity of Milwaukee, Megill proceeded to strike out DeLuca to end the game for real this time. The Brewers have a 1-0 lead in their first World Series in 44 years.

Game 2 is scheduled for Saturday at 8 p.m. ET, with Rays ace Drew Rasmussen and Brewers rookie Logan Henderson set to take the mound. Both teams are in pursuit of their first World Series title.

articles.title: Brewers withstand Rays’ comeback attempt to win 3-2 in Game 1 of World Series
articles.summary: MILWAUKEE — Trevor Megill struck out Jonny DeLuca with runners on second and third to wiggle out of a ninth-inning jam as the Milwaukee Brewers escaped with a 3-2 victory over the Tampa Bay Rays in Game 1 of the World Series on Friday night.
articles.body: MILWAUKEE — Trevor Megill struck out Jonny DeLuca with runners on second and third to wiggle out of a ninth-inning jam as the Milwaukee Brewers escaped with a 3-2 victory over the Tampa Bay Rays in Game 1 of the World Series on Friday night. DeLuca's strikeout came after Tampa Bay's Liam Hicks had grounded into an apparent game-ending double play that was overturned after a video review. Replays determined that Brewers shortstop Cooper Pratt's right foot was slightly off the bag when he reached to catch a high throw from second baseman Brice Turang. Jacob Misiorowski allowed one run over five innings to earn the win. Christian Yelich hit an RBI triple to spark a two-run rally in the first inning that put the Brewers ahead for good and delighted a sellout crowd reveling in Milwaukee’s first World Series game since 1982. Jackson Chourio and William Contreras provided two hits each, and Contreras also threw out two potential base stealers. This marks the first World Series featuring two potential first-time champions since 1980, when the Philadelphia Phillies beat the Kansas City Royals in six games. The only other major league teams without a World Series title are the Colorado Rockies, San Diego Padres and Seattle Mariners. The Game 1 winner has gone on to win the World Series 62.8% of the time. Tampa Bay trailed 3-1 and hadn't put a runner on since the sixth inning until it mounted its comeback try in the ninth. Jonathan Aranda and Chandler Simpson hit consecutive one-out singles off Megill. A double steal involving pinch-runner Jorge Mateo and Simpson put the potential tying run in scoring position with Rays slugger Junior Caminero at the plate. Caminero walked on a 3-2 pitch in the dirt to load the bases. Hicks hit a grounder to the right side, and Turang ranged well to his left to field the ball before throwing to Pratt to start what initially was ruled a game-ending double play. But a replay review determined Pratt’s right foot came off the bag as he caught Turang’s throw. Hicks was still out at first, but the Rays now had runners at second and third with the score 3-2. Megill finally closed the deal as DeLuca struck out swinging. By sweeping the two-time defending World Series champion Los Angeles Dodgers in the National League Championship Series, the Brewers had time to set up their rotation the way they wanted by handing the Game 1 start to Misiorowski, the hard-throwing NL Cy Young Award favorite. Misiorowski opened the game by throwing the fastest pitch ever delivered in a World Series game, a 103.5 mph ball to Yandy Díaz. The right-hander ended up allowing only one run over five innings with a season-low three strikeouts. While Milwaukee opened with its ace, Tampa Bay countered with Nick Martinez to give two-time All-Star pitchers Drew Rasmussen and Freddy Peralta an extra day of rest. Martinez struck out five and allowed two runs over five innings, but a slow start proved costly. Chourio lined a single to right on Martinez’s first pitch, and Yelich drove him home with a one-out triple to center. DeLuca covered 85 feet to track Yelich’s drive down but just missed making a diving catch. Yelich was batting third in the lineup for the first time since Aug. 3. The three-time All-Star and 2018 NL MVP posted the lowest on-base percentage (.315) and OPS (.692) of his career, but he has stepped up his since being named the first team captain in franchise history the final week of the regular season. He was the seventh player to triple in his first World Series plate appearance, and the first since Kansas City’s Lynn Jones in 1985, according to the Elias Sports Bureau. Contreras knocked home Yelich with a single to left that was deflected by shortstop Taylor Walls. Tampa Bay got a run back in the fourth. Aranda drew a leadoff walk and advanced to third when Caminero doubled on a liner with a 112.7 mph exit velocity that sailed over the head of center fielder Garrett Mitchell. Aranda came home on a grounder to the right side. Milwaukee extended the lead to 3-1 in the seventh. Pratt drew a leadoff walk from Steven Matz and scored from second when Chourio greeted Kevin Kelly with a two-out single to right. That insurance run proved critical.

articles.title: World Series 2026: Jacob Misiorowski throws fastest pitch in recorded Fall Classic history at 103.5 mph
articles.summary: As expected, Jacob Misiorowski brought some record heat to MLB's biggest stage.
articles.body:
As expected, Jacob Misiorowski brought some record heat to MLB's biggest stage.

The Milwaukee Brewers' ace fired a 103.5-mph fastball to Tampa Bay Rays leadoff hitter Yandy Díaz to open the 2026 World Series on Friday. It was the fastest pitch in the recorded history of the Fall Classic, according to MLB.com's Sarah Langs . MLB's pitch tracking goes back to 2008.

The previous record-holder was then-Chicago Cubs closer Aroldis Chapman in Game 2 of the 2016 World Series.

That wasn't the only history Misiorowski made Friday. Over the next five innings, he threw 38 pitches of at least 100 mph, the most in a World Series game in the tracking era, per MLB.com's Sarah Langs . He's the only pitcher to throw at least 30 such pitches in a postseason appearance, and he has done it four times.

Beyond Chapman's high-water mark, the previous record for a starting pitcher was 101.1 mph, set by Noah Syndergaard with the New York Mets in 2015. Misiorowski threw 25 pitches faster than that in Game 1.

Misiorowski finished his night with a line of 5 innings, 4 hits, 1 run, 1 walk and 3 strikeouts on 78 pitches. Between that and four strong innings from the bullpen, the Brewers won 3-2 to take a 1-0 lead in the Fall Classic .

This season has seen Misiorowski enter the record books in multiple ways when it comes to throwing the ball hard. He still hasn't topped Chapman's overall pitch speed record of 105.9 mph, but he came 0.4 mph short in June. That was the fastest pitch ever thrown by a starting pitcher and the third-hardest overall .

It also took Misiorowski only one pitch to break the MLB postseason velocity record, as his 104.8-mph fastball to open Game 1 of the NLDS represents the new high-water mark .

As impressive as Misiorowski's fastest pitches have been, where he really stands out in history is how often he hits triple digits . He had 52 pitches faster than 100 mph in Game 1 of the NLDS, then 44 in Game 1 of the NLCS. After only five postseason appearances (three starts) in 2024 and 2025, he is already second in MLB history in 100-mph pitches thrown in the postseason .

That velocity translated to historic dominance during the regular season, so much so that Misiorowski is the presumptive Cy Young winner in the National League. However, his two starts in the postseason before Friday weren't quite up to that standard.

The 6-foot-7 right-hander didn't get past the fifth inning in either of his outings against the San Diego Padres and Los Angeles Dodgers, with both teams finding ways to grind out at-bats like few clubs did against Misiorowski in the regular season. After leading MLB in whiff rate on his fastball with a ludicrous 56.3%, per Baseball Savant, Misiorowski managed only four such pitches against the Padres and five against the Dodgers.

The Brewers' World Series hopes arguably rested on him avoiding a repeat against the Rays. That worked out just fine in Game 1, even if he still got only five fastball whiffs on 25 swings.

articles.title: World Series 2026: Jacob Misiorowski finds a way, with another assist from the bullpen, to lead Brewers to Game 1 victory
articles.summary: The Brewers' ace is finding ways to get outs in the postseason, even when he doesn't have his Cy Young-caliber stuff.
articles.body:
MILWAUKEE — Jacob Misiorowski's right arm has been the figurative lightning rod for the 2026 Milwaukee Brewers. Using whatever stat you can think of — ERA, batting average against, WHIP, strikeouts and, of course, average fastball velocity by a starting pitcher — dominance has been the name of the game for the Brewers' 24-year-old flamethrower.

And while the regular season saw Misiorowski consistently dominate hitters, Milwaukee's ace has had to battle through his starts this postseason. He hasn't steamrollered his opponents this month, as opposing lineups have made him work. Even so, there's nobody the Brewers would rather have on the mound in Game 1 of the World Series.

And on Friday, when they were looking to set the tone with the franchise seeking its first World Series title, the Brewers did what they usually do in a Misiorowski start: win.

"I think the thing that I've realized the most was [that] it's October baseball," Misiorowski said after his team's 3-2 victory in Game 1 . "It doesn't matter how you get outs … just get them. There's 27 [outs] to get, and my job is to get however many I can get in my span of being out there."

It's a little difficult to believe that the Brewers are just three wins away from winning a championship, yet their best pitcher has made only three starts. And in those three starts, the opponents' plan against Misiorowski was clear. Against the Padres and Dodgers in the NLDS and NLCS, both teams' plan of attack was to grind out at-bats against the right-hander and get him out of the game early.

The AL champion Tampa Bay Rays, who have the lowest strikeout rate of any team in baseball, didn't deviate from that plan, either.

But this time around, it appeared that Misiorowski was aware of the other team's plan and wanted to use it to his advantage. He allowed Tampa to put the ball in play to stay efficient.

The first five outs of Misiorowski's night came on balls put in play. Then he struck out Jonny DeLuca for his first punchout of the game to close the second inning.

"He did great," designated hitter Christian Yelich said afterward. "He did his thing, gave us a chance to win. That's all you can ask for. He's been big for us all year. It was nice to see him get that first inning under his belt and kinda settle down."

One of the biggest knocks against Misiorowski this postseason has been the lack of length. Entering the Fall Classic, his longest start this postseason was just 4 1/3 innings in the NLCS. On Friday, he was relatively efficient through his first three innings of work, but then a lengthy fourth inning saw the Rays push across a run on a Liam Hicks groundout, and the fifth inning featured more traffic on the bases. Suddenly, it looked like Misiorowski would fail to get through five innings again.

Instead, Misiorowski got some timely help from his defense. After a leadoff single by Victor Mesa Jr., the Brewers got the first out on a tough play by David Hamilton and Jake Bauers, followed by a popout from Taylor Walls. Then catcher William Contreras threw out Mesa trying to steal third. That ended the inning and got his ace through five.

"I thought Miz was great tonight," Brewers manager Pat Murphy said postgame. "What we're used to seeing in the regular season was Miz just mowing through people and having two strikeouts an inning. That's unrealistic.

"This is the best team in the American League. They proved that during the regular season and proved that in the postseason so far. One of the ways they do that is to make contact better than anybody in baseball. For Miz to go five innings the way he did, give up only a few hard contacts, only walked one guy, I think didn't give up any free bases. … We had a lot of good performances, a lot of good things."

Misiorowski's outing marked the first time since Sept. 15 that he completed five innings and tied him with Logan Henderson for the longest outing by a Brewers starter this postseason. After setting such a high bar for himself during the regular season, tossing 5 innings with 1 run allowed on 4 hits, 1 walk and 3 strikeouts might not stand out. But the Brewers' ace is finding ways to get outs, even when he doesn't have his Cy Young-caliber stuff.

It's no secret that Misiorowski is likely fatigued. Even with 12 days off between starts, the right-hander's 188 regular-season and postseason innings in 2026 represent his most as a professional by 47 1/3 innings. While his fastball averaged around his norm for the season on Friday, he got just seven swing-and-misses.

"It's really special," reliever Aaron Ashby said. "It's a credit to him because it's his first time really having a full big-league season and then being relied on in the way that he's relied on. So just awesome to see it.

"He's a young kid, and I don't want to say it's easy to do, but he's got this freak ability to throw a baseball really hard, and he does it very efficiently. So he's got to be really, really tired to not throw the ball over 100 mph."

Even with a star like Misiorowski on their side, the Brewers' path to victory has never been placed solely on his shoulders. In fact, this postseason, Milwaukee's bullpen has shouldered the load on its ace's behalf. Sure enough, after Misiorowski got Game 1 to the sixth inning, the Brewers' electric bullpen ensured that he became the first Milwaukee starter to earn a win this postseason.

Four innings by the dominant trio of Abner Uribe, Ashby and Trevor Megill locked down the game, including a tight ninth inning , leaving the Brewers just three victories away from a World Series title. Milwaukee has not lost a Misiorowski start this postseason.

"I'm thrilled that we got wins in every game I've been in," he said. "It's been awesome to have the team behind me and being able to succeed. It's been outstanding."

articles.title: World Series 2026: William Contreras shines with his bat, his arm and his ABS challenges in Brewers' Game 1 victory
articles.summary: "I'm a player that likes to play with a lot of passion and a lot of energy, and I'm going to do that," Contreras said after Milwaukee took a 1-0 series lead.
articles.body:
MILWAUKEE — William Contreras yelled at the top of his lungs, but nobody could hear him. It was impossible to distinguish his joyous scream from the ear-splitting din shaking the very foundations of American Family Field.

But with a slight yet noticeable shake of his head, Contreras expressed himself loud and clear: Don't run on me.

"I'm a player that likes to play with a lot of passion and a lot of energy, and I'm going to do that," Contreras boasted after his Brewers' 3-2 win in Game 1 of the World Series on Friday.

Milwaukee's bowling ball of a backstop, a man shaped like a Bowser-Wario full-speed collision, had just thrown out Tampa Bay's Jonathan Aranda to end the top of the sixth inning. It was Contreras' second caught stealing in as many innings. A frame earlier, he'd tallied the final out with a frozen rope of a toss to nail Victor Mesa Jr. at third base and keep the Brewers' 2-1 lead intact. Add a pair of successful ABS challenges and two knocks, including a first-inning RBI single, and there's no doubt that Game 1 belonged to the fierce, stocky, in-command catcher from Puerto Cabello, Venezuela.

"He's incredible," Milwaukee manager Pat Murphy gushed postgame. "We wouldn't be in the position we're in without Contreras."

The Milwaukee catcher's ability to mute Tampa Bay's running game was an enormous development in Game 1. The Rays' electric baserunning helped propel them through an admittedly underwhelming American League side of this postseason bracket. An AL pennant will hang from Tropicana Field, in part, because the Rays started October a perfect 11-for-11 on stolen bases.

But Contreras and these Brewers are a different beast. Milwaukee is crisper on the margins, sharper on defense, harder to take advantage of, more detail-oriented and better at executing than either of the clubs Tampa dispatched on its way to this World Series. The Brewers play with an unrelenting intensity, one perfectly exemplified by Contreras, who is equal parts emotional and laser-focused.

"I think just his competitiveness and the way that he's willing to bring it every day. He wants to compete every single day, every moment," Brewers captain Christian Yelich said of Contreras during the NLCS. "He's the fire of our team."

Despite Milwaukee's aggressive style of play, not many of their key position players come across on the field as extroverted showmen. Yelich is a metronome; so is second baseman Brice Turang. NLCS MVP Jake Bauers is busy being stuck in flowstate. Young star Jackson Chourio will raise his energy to match a moment, but he's far from the most expressive character.

Contreras, meanwhile, has been known to bash himself on the helmet with his own bat after missing pitches he believes he should have clobbered. After a big hit, he'll flip his bat or emphatically pound his chest or flex and yell. He did the latter two after his timely RBI poke in the first inning Friday.

As Contreras strode to the plate for the first World Series plate appearance of his career, he did so beneath a crowd roaring over Milwaukee's first Fall Classic run in 44 years. Yelich, batting third for the first time in months, had cranked a ball into the right-center gap for an RBI triple. He stood on third with a man down as a valuable early insurance run.

Everybody in the ballpark, including the Rays, must have known that Contreras would be hacking. This season, only five qualified hitters swung more often at 0-0 pitches in the strike zone with runners in scoring position. Anything in the strike zone from Tampa Bay starter Nick Martinez, and Contreras' bat was coming off his shoulder.

Martinez's cutter backed up and caught too much dish. Contreras uncoiled and ripped one 108.4 mph right at shortstop Taylor Walls, but it was too hot to handle, and the ball ricocheted off Walls' mitt and into the outfield.

"God was able to gift me that one today, a complete game on both sides," Contreras said afterward through team interpreter Daniel de Mondesert.

Contreras was also nails with his ABS challenges. He head-tapped twice in Game 1, earning the overturn each time. With likely NL Cy Young Award winner Jacob Misiorowski less than his best , Contreras stole a second strike in the third inning, leading to a strikeout. With a runner on in the sixth, he avoided a 2-0 count with another challenge.

"In regards to the ABS, going through a good moment right now, and I think the ABS is kind of similar to hitting in a season," he explained via de Mondesert. "You might go through a slump. Right now, I think I'm going through a good moment with it, and I've got to take advantage of that."

The Brewers certainly took advantage of Contreras' magnificent performance to snag an early series lead. It was yet another outstanding showing for a player once discarded by the Atlanta Braves in a three-team trade because they were skeptical he'd ever develop the defensive skills to handle a staff. Now Contreras is the backstop for baseball's best run-prevention unit and tied for the lead in hits this postseason.

His 1.184 OPS is tops among players who reached the championship series. He has simply been the best, most productive hitter on the National League champion. Defensively, too, he has been a difference-maker. Murphy, though, says it's even more than that.

"The side that you can't measure, I don't know what his numbers are, but he does so much for the team," he said.

Thanks to Contreras, the Brewers are here and now, three wins away from winning it all.

articles.title: World Series 2026: Rays come up short on coin-flip plays and defensive near-misses in Game 1 loss to Brewers
articles.summary: It's hard not to view Game 1 as a missed opportunity for Tampa Bay, especially given the 3-2 final score.
articles.body:
MILWAUKEE — In a World Series between two clubs that thrive on mastering the little things, it was only right that Game 1's most significant plays were determined by the slimmest of margins.

No major-league team had a better record in one-run games in the regular season than the Tampa Bay Rays at 25-14, one of the many indicators of the club's comfort when it comes to executing deftly on both sides of the ball. But on Friday at American Family Field, it was the Brewers who were on the right side of just enough coin-flip plays en route to a 3-2 Game 1 victory that gave the sellout crowd of 43,250 plenty to cheer for in the city's first World Series game in 44 years.

From the very start of Game 1, the scales seemed to tip ever-so-slightly in Milwaukee's favor. Yandy Díaz lifted the third pitch from Brewers ace Jacob Misiorowski deep into right field, where it landed in Sal Frelick's glove, though it would've been a home run in 10 of 30 MLB ballparks, according to Statcast. Jonathan Aranda and Chandler Simpson followed with a pair of singles to give Junior Caminero a golden opportunity to jump ahead early, but Caminero lined one to shortstop Cooper Pratt, who tossed it swiftly to second base to double off Aranda and end the inning.

To absolutely no one's surprise, Jackson Chourio swung at the first pitch from Rays starter Nick Martinez and dumped one into right field to lead off the game for Milwaukee, easing some of the tension that had built when multiple baserunners reached against Misiorowski. That tension transformed into ecstasy when captain Christian Yelich drove an 0-2 cutter from Martinez into the right-center-field gap. Jonny DeLuca raced over and laid out to try to make the grab, but to no avail; the ball found the grass just beyond his outstretched glove.

"I thought Jonny covered a lot of ground right there to even make that play close," manager Kevin Cash said afterward.

Only three outfielders (Pete Crow-Armstrong, Ceddanne Rafaela and Michael Harris II) racked up more Outs Above Average than DeLuca in the regular season. The notion that he could have made a spectacular play to rob Yelich was entirely plausible. But he did not, so it was 1-0 Brewers, with Yelich scampering to third base for his first triple since July 22.

That brought Tampa Bay's infield in as it tried to limit the damage with a runner on third and just one out. So when William Contreras scalded a first-pitch cutter, shortstop Taylor Walls — whose anticipation and first step are about as good as you'll see from an infielder — did not have enough time to react. Contreras' 108.4 mph screamer tipped off Walls' glove and sizzled into left field to drive in Yelich and make it 2-0 Milwaukee. Martinez then struck out Brice Turang and Garrett Mitchell with his terrific changeup, but the feeling in the Tampa Bay dugout as he walked off the mound was a rather unfamiliar one: It was the first time since Sept. 2 that the Rays had allowed multiple runs in the first inning.

If these early near-misses on defense weren't frustrating enough, the Rays proceeded to endure a series of close encounters with run-scoring opportunities, only to cross the plate just twice by the end of the night. Caminero managed to break through in the fourth with his hardest-hit ball of the postseason, a 112.7-mph laser beam launched over center fielder Garrett Mitchell's head for a double that moved Jonathan Aranda, who'd led off with a walk, to third. That set up a Liam Hicks RBI groundout that made it 2-1, but ultimately, the fourth inning was one of several unfulfilled chances to add on more and make Milwaukee sweat.

With Díaz facing Misiorowski for the third time with two outs in the fifth, Victor Mesa Jr. attempted to steal third base on an 0-2 count, only to be cut down by Contreras with a perfect throw and an even more perfect tag by third baseman David Hamilton.

"Ultimately, Victor is really competing, trying to do something to make something happen, put a little pressure on the defense," Cash said afterward. "And it didn't work in our favor."

That ended the inning and Misiorowski's outing after just 78 pitches , as he made way for the Brewers' outstanding bullpen to handle the final four frames.

With Martinez keeping the Milwaukee bats quiet from innings two-through-five, another chance for the Rays' offense surfaced in the sixth, when Aranda notched a one-out single against Abner Uribe. But on a full count to Simpson, the slow-footed Aranda took off for second, counting on the contact-maven Simpson to put the bat on the ball. Instead, Uribe's slider darted down and in and coaxed a rare whiff for strike three. Aranda — the active player with the most career plate appearances without a stolen base — was thrown out at second for a caught stealing in the book, but a failed hit-and-run in reality and the end of the inning.

Before Friday, Simpson had struck out just once this postseason, a strikeout looking against Gerrit Cole in ALDS Game 1 that required an ABS challenge to overturn a called ball into strike three. In Game 1 of the Fall Classic, Misiorowski and Uribe combined to hand Simpson his first multi-strikeout game since June 9. It was that kind of night for Tampa Bay.

After Chourio tacked on an insurance run in the seventh to make it 3-1 Brewers, the final fit of frustration for the Rays came in a chaotic top of the ninth inning . Tampa Bay managed to load the bases with one out against Milwaukee closer Trevor Megill, offering one last glimmer of hope to steal Game 1 on the road. Hicks then grounded into what looked like a game-ending double play — so much so that the postgame processes began to commence, with a horde of league officials and television crews hustling onto the field — only to have the play overturned by replay.

It turned out Pratt's foot was off second base, which meant Caminero was safe at second, and only Hicks was out at first. With that, it was 3-2 with the tying run on third and the go-ahead run on second. That glimmer had grown to a full-blown beam of possibility — but then DeLuca flailed at a curveball from Megill for a game-ending strikeout.

It's hard not to view how Game 1 unfolded as something of a missed opportunity for Tampa Bay, especially given the final margin.

Viewed more generously, though the Rays hung tough with the NL champs without using any of their top relievers, while Milwaukee leaned heavily on its top bullpen arms, a combination that could pay dividends as the series progresses. The Rays also put together some quality at-bats against Misiorowski and Co. They did not look overmatched but simply failed to capitalize. Add the starting pitching advantage Tampa Bay would seem to have the next couple of games with Drew Rasmussen and Freddy Peralta, and there is undoubtedly a path back into this series for the Rays.

But against a team like the Brewers, it will take far fewer missteps than what we saw on Friday.

articles.title: World Series: Milwaukee Brewers beat Tampa Bay Rays 3-2 in opening game
articles.summary: The Milwaukee Brewers beat the Tampa Bay Rays 3-2 in the opening game of the best-of-seven World Series as both sides aim for their first title.
articles.body:
Milwaukee Brewers starting pitcher Jacob Misiorowski threw the fastest recorded pitch in World Series history as his side began the best-of-seven season finale with a win.

The right-hander played a starring role in the 3-2 win at home to the Tampa Bay Rays, in the first match of the 122nd World Series.

It is only the second time in more than a century that neither side contesting the World Series has won the title before.

A sell-out crowd watched the Brewers in only their second appearance in the finale of the Major League Baseball season, and their first since losing to the St Louis Cardinals in 1982.

Milwaukee's American Family Field has 41,900 seats but with standing-room-only tickets available for the 'Fall Classic', 43,250 fans packed in to see the game.

"It was amazing - just to have the city behind me, it means the world, we couldn't ask for anything better," said Misiorowski.

The Brewers host the second match of the best-of-seven series on Saturday before the teams move to Florida for three games, then return to Milwaukee for the final two matches, if needed.

Misiorowski, 24, became the youngest starter since 1997 to win a World Series opener, after restricting the Rays to just one run in five innings.

His fastest pitch at 103.5 mph beat the previous mark of 103.2 mph set by Aroldis Chapman of the Chicago Cubs in 2016 - though speeds have only been recorded since 2008.

Brewers designated hitter Christian Yelich also played a key role, scoring one run and driving in another as they took a 3-1 lead.

The Rays added one run in the final inning and had a runner on third base as they pushed to level the score, but Milwaukee closed out victory.

"It feels great. The guys settled in right away and did a great job," Yelich said. "We've still got a ways to go but nice to get that first one."

The Brewers made the World Series by beating the Los Angeles Dodgers 4-0 to claim the National League title, while the Rays clinched the American League pennant with a 4-2 win over the Cleveland Guardians to reach the post-season finale for only the third time.

The Rays lost to the Philadelphia Phillies in the 2008 World Series and the Dodgers in 2020, but manager Kevin Cash took solace from the fact that they tested the Brewers on Friday.

"We came up a little bit short, but there's some benefit maybe from a loss," said Cash.

articles.title: DEPROGRAMMED: He was headed for the MLB. Instead he stepped up to the plate for God
articles.summary: Nehemiah Toles walked away from top college baseball offers and MLB scouts after hearing God's voice in a hotel room following a championship game.
articles.body: Star outfielder Nehemiah Toles had multiple Division-I college baseball offers and MLB scouts watching him as he neared high school graduation, but he turned all of it down in pursuit of his purpose — preaching the Gospel to bring America’s youth to Jesus. "It's the scariest thing to be gifted at something that God did not call you to… Baseball was my passion, it wasn't my purpose," Toles told Fox News Digital. "When I stand before God… and he looks at me, he's gonna say well done, good and faithful servant. How did hitting home runs, how would that have served Him?" he continued. FALCONS ROOKIE ZACHARIAH BRANCH SAYS CHRISTIAN FAITH, DAILY DEVOTIONALS FUEL HIS NFL JOURNEY Toles, who now runs his own ministry traveling across the U.S. to preach the Gospel, grew up in a household with a pastor father transitioning to be an evangelist. Although surrounded by faith in his home, he admits to thinking religion and following God was "corny" during his youth. The former baseball player revealed that he used the sport as a "coping mechanism" while dealing with anxiety and depression that peaked in school during the pandemic of 2020. "From 13 years old to 16 years old… I felt like I struggled to connect with people, struggled to just articulate my thoughts. And so… I went back to church, [and] before I even started worshiping or anything like that, I felt the presence of God just hit me. All my anxiety, all my depression left, and I had tried everything else and nothing else was working," Toles continued. JUST 5 MINUTES OF PRAYER COULD HAVE SURPRISING HEALTH BENEFITS, STUDY FINDS Toles detailed one of his first experiences receiving college offers during a championship game while ranked the top outfielder in the state of Ohio, running to second base chalking up reddish brown dust in the air with the impact of each cleated step, seeing his coach on the phone from under the shadow of his baseball cap, rounding third base and finishing a home run before making it to the dugout. "I'm in the dugout. And [my coach] he's like… before [you] touched home plate, three Division-I coaches had just confirmed," Toles continued. He described the elation on his parents' faces and recalled his father’s tears at the news of the offers from Yale and a handful of other universities, all right before he heard the voice of God later that night alone in his room. LOUISIANA FOOTBALL PHENOM PEYTON HOUSTON CREDITS FAITH, FAMILY FOR HIS REMARKABLE SUCCESS "[In] the hotel room that night and I felt like the Lord had spoke[n] to me, like, 'Is that enough? Was that what you were looking for? Like, is this ever, is it going to be enough?'" he said. Toles described serving at a community event helping children in need shortly after that game, wrestling between both destinies, finding that serving those kids was "something deeper" and "more satisfying" to him than hitting home runs or getting top college offers. "I felt like God was calling me into full-time ministry and so… [During that] exact event, I went back to the green room and I called half of the Division-I coaches and told them I'm not going to come to their college, I'm going full-time into ministry," Toles said. NFL LINEBACKER AND AMATEUR PREACHER DEMARIO DAVIS DELIVERS AMAZING SERMON ON WINNING AND LIFE Despite tension with his family and multiple hard conversations with various adults, from guidance counselors to coaches and more imploring Toles to reconsider his decision, he stood firm. TONY DUNGY TELLS SAGE STEELE THAT NBC WASN'T HAPPY WITH HIS PRO-LIFE VIEWS: 'THEY KNEW WHERE I STOOD' "Everything that the world had offered me didn't satisfy me… I remember feeling so deceived and feeling so frustrated, because doing the things that people had told me to do [that] they said they would make me happy and would fulfill me… didn't," he added. Toles endured pressure from all sides that eventually led him to question his choice, but when he asked God, he heard his voice clearer than ever. "He made it so evident to me, He [said], obedience to me will always be insanity to the world," Toles said. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

articles.title: Rob Manfred Addresses MLB Salary Cap Stance as Brewers, Rays Compete for World Series Title
articles.summary: MLB commissioner Rob Manfred continued the league's push for a salary cap prior to Game 1 of the World Series on Friday night.
articles.body:
MLB commissioner Rob Manfred continued the league's push for a salary cap prior to Game 1 of the World Series on Friday night.

Speaking to reporters prior to the start of the Tampa Bay Rays-Milwaukee Brewers series, Manfred reiterated his stance on behalf of the owners that a salary cap is needed despite having two small-market teams playing for a championship.

"I think it shows that we leave a lot on the table in some of our smaller markets by not having them have an opportunity to compete on a regular basis," Manfred said. "The Brewers have been a well-run franchise forever. It's been 40 years since we're here. Once every 40 years is not enough."

Manfred went on to say there is "an unprecedented level of unanimity among ownership" to bring a salary cap to MLB.

Even though Manfred made the point that Milwaukee is in the World Series for the first time since 1982, the Rays are making their third appearance in the Fall Classic since 2008. This is their second time winning the American League championship in seven seasons.

The combined $242 million in payrolls for the Brewers and Rays is the lowest for a World Series matchup in the last 10 seasons. It marks the second time during that span the combined payroll was under $300 million, along with 2020.

MLB laid out an initial proposal with a salary cap in May that starts at $245.3 million and contains a salary floor of at least $171.2 million. Only seven teams exceeded $245.3 million in payroll this season, while 15 teams were under $171.2 million in roster spending.

Of the top five teams in payroll spending this season, the Los Angeles Dodgers were the only one that reached the league championship series. Two of them — New York Mets and Toronto Blue Jays — didn't even make the playoffs.

Three of the bottom seven teams in payroll spending — Rays, Chicago White Sox and Cleveland Guardians — all made the playoffs. The Rays and Guardians met in the ALCS.

Milwaukee ranks 19th in payroll spending and was in the NLCS last year before getting to the World Series this year.

Manfred's comments come amid what is expected to be a prolonged labor battle between MLB and the MLB Players Association. The current collective bargaining agreement expires at 11:59 p.m. ET on Dec. 1.

MLB's last work stoppage was the 2021-22 lockout that lasted 99 days and pushed opening day back one week from March 31 to April 7.

There hasn't been a work stoppage that resulted in games lost since the 1994-95 player strike, which was also the last time owners dug in their heels for a salary cap.

articles.title: The Most Important Win In The World Series May Surprise You
articles.summary: An analysis of 31 years of World Series data reveals which games matter most, how victories affect championship odds, and what mathematics says about winning...
articles.body:
The 2026 World Series was already historic before the first pitch. For the first time since 1980, two franchises that have never won a championship will compete. The Milwaukee Brewers and Tampa Bay Rays, representing two of Major League Baseball's smaller markets and operating with relatively modest payrolls , have overcome some of the sport's wealthiest competitors to reach baseball's biggest stage. Regardless of the outcome, one franchise will celebrate its first World Series title.

For both teams, the stakes could hardly be higher. Every victory brings a franchise closer to a championship that has eluded it throughout its history. Yet the significance of individual World Series victories is rarely considered equal.

Yet the relative importance of these victories is less obvious than it might seem. Is winning Game 1 particularly consequential? Does Game 3 represent a critical turning point? Or does the importance of a victory increase as the series approaches its conclusion? Which World Series win matters most?

To investigate, I analyzed 175 games from the 31 World Series played between 1995 and 2025, using historical records compiled by Retrosheet . I examined how frequently the winner of each game ultimately became champion, how those probabilities varied with the series score, and how the historical outcomes compared with the mathematical probabilities of a best-of-seven series between evenly matched teams.

The analysis reveals several intriguing patterns, including differences between historical championship rates and the probabilities implied by the structure of the series itself. Understanding those differences requires examining what it actually means for one World Series victory to matter more than another.

World Series Game 1 Has Been a Strong Historical Indicator of Championship Success

The analysis begins in 1995, the inaugural season of Major League Baseball's Wild Card Era . Between 1995 and 2025, the team that won Game 1 went on to win the World Series in 24 of 31 instances, representing a championship rate of 77.4%. That was the highest observed rate among winners of the first five games.

Game 2 winners became champions 64.5% of the time, compared with 61.3% for Game 3 winners. The corresponding rates for Games 4 and 5 were 67.7% and 68.0%. The historical rates increased for the final two games. Game 6 winners became champions in 82.4% of the series that reached a sixth game, while every Game 7 winner necessarily became champion.

The Game 1 result is particularly noteworthy. Winning the opener has historically been associated with a substantially higher championship rate than winning Game 3, despite both games occurring in every World Series. (The Brewers clinched Game 1 Friday night.) The historical association does not establish that winning Game 1 produces a greater increase in championship probability than winning another game. Stronger teams may be more likely to win both the opener and the championship, while individual World Series outcomes remain subject to considerable randomness. A mathematical comparison helps distinguish the significance of a victory from its observed association with the eventual championship.

What Mathematics Says About Winning World Series Game 1

Consider a World Series between two evenly matched teams, each with an independent 50% probability of winning any individual game. Under these assumptions, both teams begin with a 50% chance of winning the championship. After winning Game 1, a team's championship probability rises to 65.625%. After losing, it falls to 34.375%. Winning the opener therefore increases championship probability by 15.625 percentage points relative to the pre-series position.

However, there is another way to measure the importance of Game 1: compare the championship probabilities associated with its two possible outcomes. Winning produces a 65.625% championship probability, while losing produces a 34.375% probability. The difference is 31.25 percentage points. This difference is the game's championship-probability swing. The measure captures how much the result matters when comparing a victory with a defeat from the same starting position. It can be calculated for every possible series score and provides a consistent framework for evaluating the mathematical stakes of individual games.

The observed historical rate of 77.4% exceeds that benchmark by approximately 11.8 percentage points. Yet the historical sample includes teams of different strengths, and the difference is compatible with sampling uncertainty. More importantly, the theoretical Game 1 probability provides a baseline for examining whether other World Series victories can have greater mathematical consequences.

Why the Series Score Matters More In World Series Game 3

Game 3 provides a particularly revealing example because its importance depends on the results of the preceding two games. If the World Series is tied 1–1 entering Game 3, the winner takes a 2–1 lead.

Under the evenly matched model, that team has a 68.75% probability of winning the championship. The losing team, now trailing 1–2, has a 31.25% championship probability. The difference is 37.5 percentage points, exceeding the 31.25-point swing associated with Game 1. Consequently, a Game 3 victory in a tied series has greater mathematical consequences than a Game 1 victory.

The calculation changes when a team enters Game 3 already leading 2–0. A victory gives that team a commanding 3–0 advantage and a 93.75% probability of becoming champion. A defeat leaves it leading 2–1, with a championship probability of 68.75% representing a difference of 25 percentage points. The same 25-point swing applies to a team entering Game 3 trailing 0–2. Winning improves its championship probability to 31.25%, while losing reduces it to 6.25%. These findings reveal why the probability of winning the championship after a Game 3 victory cannot be fully understood without considering the preceding results.

The historical data provide an additional perspective. Among the 16 World Series that entered Game 3 tied 1–1, the Game 3 winner eventually became champion 11 times. The observed rate of 68.75% matches the theoretical probability exactly. Although notable, that agreement should not be interpreted as evidence that the model perfectly describes postseason baseball. With only 16 observations, the historical estimate has considerable uncertainty.

The experience of teams entering Game 3 with a two-game deficit is similarly revealing. Of the eight teams that won Game 3 after falling behind 0–2, only one ultimately won the championship. The practical meaning of a victory therefore depends heavily on the team's position when the game begins.

Importantly, there is a distinction between the probability of becoming champion after a victory and the magnitude of the probability swing. A team already leading 2–0 can have a very high championship probability after another victory, even though that victory produces a smaller probability swing than winning Game 3 in a tied series.

How the Mathematical Stakes Change in World Series Games 4 Through 7

The importance of a victory becomes increasingly dependent on the series score as the World Series progresses. Game 4 offers four possible starting positions. Under the evenly matched model, winning Game 4 when the series stands 2–1 or 1–2 produces a championship-probability swing of 37.5 percentage points. When the series stands 3–0 or 0–3, the swing is considerably smaller, at 12.5 percentage points.

Game 5 presents an even greater contrast. With the series tied 2–2, the winner moves ahead 3–2 and has a 75% probability of becoming champion. The loser, now trailing 2–3, has a championship probability of 25%. The resulting 50-percentage-point swing exceeds the corresponding value of any game in the first four contests. However, when Game 5 begins with one team leading 3–1, the probability swing is only 25 percentage points.

Game 6 has a different mathematical structure because it can occur only when the series stands 3–2. A victory by the leading team secures the championship, while a defeat forces Game 7. From either team's perspective, the difference between winning and losing Game 6 is 50 percentage points.

Finally, Game 7 offers the maximum possible probability swing of 100 percentage points. Its winner becomes champion, while its loser is eliminated.

These results demonstrate that the mathematical consequences of a World Series victory cannot be determined from the game number alone. The series score establishes how much championship probability is at stake, and the largest swings generally occur when the series remains closely contested.

The historical record offers a compelling case for the importance of winning Game 1. Since 1995, teams that won the World Series opener have gone on to capture 77.4% of championships, the highest rate among winners of the first five games. Yet the mathematical analysis reveals that the consequences of a victory depend heavily on the series score. A win in a closely contested series can produce a substantially greater change in championship probability than an identical result earlier in the competition.

Game 7 represents the ultimate example, with a single victory determining the championship. However, its relatively low probability of occurring introduces an important consideration. When the likelihood of reaching each game is incorporated into the analysis, all seven scheduled games have precisely the same expected championship-probability swing under the evenly matched model. This finding reconciles two seemingly contradictory observations: later games can carry considerably greater consequences, even as every potential game begins with the same expected mathematical importance.

For the Brewers and Rays, the distinction offers an intriguing perspective on a World Series that will produce a first-time champion. The historical record suggests that winning the opener is associated with considerable championship success. The mathematics, however, leaves room for the significance of each subsequent victory to change as the series unfolds.

articles.title: Misiorowski, Megill React to Brewers' Win and Dramatic Replay vs. Rays in MLB World Series Game 1
articles.summary: Despite a tense ninth inning that saw a potential game-ending double play overturned on replay, the Milwaukee Brewers held on for a 3-2 win over the Tampa Bay Rays in Game 1 of the World Series.
articles.body:
Despite a tense ninth inning that saw a potential game-ending double play overturned on replay, the Milwaukee Brewers held on for a 3-2 win over the Tampa Bay Rays in Game 1 of the World Series.

Brewers ace Jacob Misiorowski, who got the win after allowing one run in five innings, called his moment in Game 1 "everything I dreamed of" and being able to do it in Milwaukee made it more special.

"It's really cool that we got to do it here in Milwaukee," Misiorowski said after the win. "It's been awesome to feel the city and feel just the atmosphere they've been creating."

Brewers closer Trevor Megill had to do more work than he originally thought after the umpires overturned a double play because shortstop Cooper Pratt's foot came off the second-base bag before he caught the ball.

The overturned call gave the Rays runners at second and third with two outs. Megill didn't waver in the moment, getting Jonny DeLuca to strike out to end the game.

"You got to think worst-case scenario there," Megill said of his reaction to the Rays' challenge. "I thought the challenge was at first base, maybe a bobble or something. But it was pretty clear once the replay went up that it was on the play at second base and, zoomed in, didn't look too good."

Megill cited his first curveball against DeLuca, which was a called strike that evened the count at 2-2, as a crucial moment in the at-bat.

"Anytime you can land a curveball at the bottom right there like that, it definitely sets up your next one," Megill said. "It's just pitching and trusting what William (Contreras) is putting down back there."

The next pitch after that was another curveball in the dirt that DeLuca chased for strike three. It gave the Brewers their first victory in a World Series game since Oct. 17, 1982.

"It's good to get the first win out of the way," Megill told reporters. "That's where all the nerves are at in this first game. A lot of anticipation and buildup to where we're at right now. To get that first one out of the way with a win is a big step in the right direction there."

Megill did allow his first run of the postseason on the Hicks groundout. This was also his first game allowing a hit since Game 1 of the NLDS against the San Diego Padres.

Even with the minor blip from Megill, the Brewers' bullpen allowed just one run with six strikeouts over four innings. Their relievers ERA sits at 1.41 with 25 hits allowed in 44.2 innings over the entire postseason.

Milwaukee has now won six straight playoff games and is 8-1 overall this postseason. The Brewers will go for a 2-0 series lead against the Rays in Game 2 on Saturday at 8 p.m. ET.
